intro: The past perfect (had + past participle) is the “past of the past”: it shows that one past action happened before another past action. You need it to tell stories clearly and to report what people said.
objectifs: Form the past perfect in all its forms and recognise the contraction 'd.
Show that one past action happened before another, especially with when, after, before, by the time, already and never.
Know when the past perfect is necessary and when the past simple is enough.
Meet the past perfect continuous (had been + -ing) for duration up to a past moment.

texte: We make the past perfect with had (the same for every subject) and the past participle: I had finished, she had left, they had gone.
In speech, had becomes 'd: I'd, you'd, she'd, we'd, they'd. Careful: 'd can also mean would (I'd like). The next word tells you: 'd + participle = had (I'd seen); 'd + base verb = would (I'd see).
Negative: hadn't + participle. Question: Had + subject + participle? Short answer: Yes, she had. / No, she hadn't.

lignes: The film had started when we arrived.
Where had she put the keys?
Yes, subject + had. / No, subject + hadn't.
Had they left? – Yes, they had.

texte: When we tell a story in the past simple, we use the past perfect to go back to an even earlier action. Imagine a timeline: action 1 (past perfect) → action 2 (past simple) → now.
Compare: “When I arrived, the train left” = the train left at the moment I arrived (or just after). “When I arrived, the train had left” = the train was already gone; I missed it.
exemples: When we got to the cinema, the film had already started.
The film started first, then we arrived.
She was nervous because she had never flown before.
I recognised him because I had seen his photo.
They had sold the house by the time we called.
The sale happened before the call.

texte: Some words often go with the past perfect because they show that something came earlier: already, just, never… before, by the time, by + date, until, after, before, when, because.
By the time is very typical: “By the time the police arrived, the thieves had escaped.”

lignes: I had just sat down when the phone rang.
I had never seen snow before that trip.
By the time I woke up, she had gone.
By 2010, he had written five novels.
After she had finished, she went out.

sections.titre: When the past simple is enough
texte: If we tell actions in the order they happened, the past simple is enough: “I opened the door, switched on the light and sat down.”

With after and before, the order is already clear, so the past perfect is possible but not necessary: “After she finished / had finished, she went out.” The past perfect stresses that the first action was completely finished.

A common mistake is to use the past perfect for the “distant past”. Distance in time doesn't matter; the order between two past moments does. “The Romans built this bridge” (not “had built”) if no later past event is mentioned.
exemples: I got up, had a shower and left.
Before I left, I checked the windows.
Before makes the order clear: past simple is fine.

sections.titre: Reported speech and the past perfect continuous
texte: We also use the past perfect when we report words or thoughts in the past: “She said she had lost her phone” (her words: “I've lost / I lost my phone”). Lessons 104 and 105 go further.

The past perfect continuous (had been + -ing) shows that an activity continued up to a moment in the past, just as the present perfect continuous does up to now: “We had been waiting for two hours when the bus finally arrived.” It can also explain past signs: “Her eyes were red: she had been crying.”
exemples: He told me he had already paid.
Reported speech: one step back in time.
I had been working there for ten years when the company closed.
Duration up to a past moment.
The ground was wet. It had been raining.
Past signs of an earlier activity.

formule: had + past participle (When I arrived, the train had left.)
prononciation: Had is weak in the middle of a sentence: /həd/ or /əd/, and often contracted to 'd /d/: “she'd gone” /ʃiːd ɡɒn/.
The 'd is very light: listen to the difference between “I left” and “I'd left”. The /d/ links to the next word: “I'd already” /aɪd ɔːlˈredi/.
hadn't /ˈhædnt/ is always stressed: “I HADN'T seen it.”
Say by the time as one block /baɪ ðə ˈtaɪm/, with the stress on time.
erreurs: When I arrived, the train left already.
When I arrived, the train had already left.
The earlier action (the train leaving) takes the past perfect.
A single dated fact is past simple; the past perfect needs another past reference point.
After had, use the participle (gone), not the past simple.
I didn't know him because I never met him before.
I didn't know him because I had never met him before.
Experience before a past moment: had never + participle.
By the time we arrived, they finished dinner.
By the time we arrived, they had finished dinner.
By the time + the earlier action in the past perfect.
He said he has lost his job.
He said he had lost his job.
After a reporting verb in the past, go one step back: has lost → had lost.

dialogue.contexte: Lyon, Monday morning. Chloé tells her colleague Malik about her disappointing weekend in Geneva.
lignes: A disaster! When we got to the station, our train had already left.
The train left before they arrived.
Oh no! Hadn't you checked the time?
Negative question in the past perfect.
We had, but the company had changed the timetable and nobody had told us.
Short answer “We had”, then two earlier actions.
Back to the main story: past simple.
We took the next one. By the time we arrived, the museum had closed.
What a shame. Had you been to Geneva before?
No, never. But the lake was beautiful, so it wasn't all bad.
It wasn't all bad = there were good things too.

mots: by the time
By the time I arrived, everyone had left.
when, at the moment that (something had already happened)
realise
I realised I had left my passport at home.
to suddenly understand or notice (US: realize)
previously
She had previously worked in Dakar.
before the time you are talking about
miss
We missed the bus because we had overslept.
to be too late for a bus, train, etc.
oversleep
I had overslept, so I was late.
to sleep longer than you planned
timetable
They had changed the timetable.
a list of times when buses, trains or classes happen (US: schedule)
discover
The police discovered that he had lied.
to find out something you didn't know
turn out
It turned out that she had already paid.
to be found to be true in the end

exercices.consigne: Write the action that happened first.
items: When I got home, my sister had cooked dinner.
My sister cooked dinner.
He had left before I called him.
He left.
The shop had closed when we arrived.
The shop closed.
I realised I had forgotten my bag.
I forgot my bag.

exercices.consigne: Put the verb in brackets in the past perfect.
items: When we arrived, the concert ___ (start).
had started
I was hungry because I ___ (not / eat) all day.
hadn't eaten
___ you ___ (meet) her before the party?
Had … met
She ___ (never / see) the sea before that holiday.
had never seen
By 9 p.m., they ___ (finish) the work.
had finished

exercices.consigne: Put one verb in the past simple and the other in the past perfect.
items: When I (get) to the bank, it (close).
got … had closed
She (be) sad because her cat (disappear).
was … had disappeared
We (not / recognise) him because he (grow) a beard.
didn't recognise … had grown
By the time the taxi (arrive), we (decide) to walk home.
arrived … had decided

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: When I arrived, the meeting already finished.
When I arrived, the meeting had already finished.
She had wrote the letter before lunch.
She had written the letter before lunch.
I had bought this car in 2019.
I bought this car in 2019.
He told me he has seen the film.
He told me he had seen the film.

exercices.consigne: Join the two sentences into one, using the word in brackets and the past perfect.
items: The bus left. Then we arrived. (When … already)
When we arrived, the bus had already left.
I ate poutine for the first time on that trip. (never … before)
I had never eaten poutine before that trip.
She said: “I've lost my keys.” (She told me…)
She told me (that) she had lost her keys.
It started raining two hours before we left. It was still raining. (had been)
It had been raining for two hours when we left.

exercices.consigne: In 4–5 sentences, tell the story of a day when everything went wrong. Use the past perfect at least three times (already, never… before, by the time…).
items: Example answer

Last Monday was terrible. When I woke up, I realised my alarm hadn't rung. By the time I got to the station, my train had already left. When I finally arrived at work, the meeting had started. I had never felt so embarrassed before.

a_retenir: Form: had + past participle, the same for every subject; contraction 'd.
Use: the earlier of two past actions (the “past of the past”).
Signals: already, just, never… before, by the time, by + time, after, before.
No past perfect for a single dated fact or a story told in order: use the past simple.
Past perfect continuous (had been + -ing): duration up to a past moment.
